units: a still stretch of water lies in the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds
its surface used to be clear and is now covered with a greenish film
lasting heat speeds up the loss of water through evaporation
the dissolved minerals grow more concentrated in what water is left
the nearby ground dries out and splits into brittle pieces
vegetation rotting on the bed gives off a repellent smell
the water insects vanish from the place
the birds that fed there desert the bank
the spring lower down supplies almost no water to the crops
the growers sink deeper wells and draw down the buried reserve
text: Down in a hollow ringed with reeds lies a motionless sheet of water. It was formerly transparent; now a greenish film stretches right across it. The cause is straightforward. Persistent heat, week upon week, draws the water off into the atmosphere, and everything dissolved within it grows concentrated in whatever remains. Around the rim the ground desiccates and splits into brittle flakes underfoot. Vegetation decomposes on the bed and releases a smell repellent enough to drive you backwards. The insects that once inhabited the shallows have disappeared, and the birds that fed upon them no longer descend to the bank. Further down the slope, the spring that watered the plots barely trickles, so the growers sink deeper wells, and the water concealed underground subsides further still.

units: the streets overheat because they have been covered with tar and concrete
the air there becomes unfit to breathe as soon as the sun strikes
cases of illness brought on by heat are multiplying
air conditioning is put forward as the answer to the problem
an air conditioner throws outside the heat it takes from inside
this equipment swallows a considerable amount of energy
the writer proposes planting dense trees along the busy roads
he proposes making school yards absorbent and laying pale surfaces
he calls for water points where people are kept waiting
he holds that these measures call for no new technique but for a budget
text: Let us be blunt for a moment. Our streets overheat because we have covered them over with tar and concrete. Once the sun strikes them the air is hardly fit to breathe, and afterwards we affect surprise that people keep collapsing in the heat. Air conditioning, we are assured, will settle the matter. It settles nothing whatever: it discharges outdoors the very heat it strips from indoors, and it swallows an astonishing quantity of power. The way out is duller and older than that. Plant dense lines of trees along the busiest thoroughfares. Break up the school yards so that rainfall soaks in. Lay pale surfaces that throw the glare back upwards. Provide clean water wherever people are kept standing about. None of this awaits a technique nobody has invented; it awaits a budget.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman in charge of a measuring station climbs each week to a rocky bowl
the man before her wrote down ice thicknesses by hand
she now receives readings that sensors send up on their own
the ice was once hard and faintly blue underfoot
the surface today is soft and gives way under the boot spikes
the front of the glacier was sharp and is now a thinned tongue
crumbling gravel streaks that tongue
she also watches two facing slopes of the same range
the slope open to the sun loses its ice far faster than the other
she holds that this gap teaches more than an overall average
text: Once a week the woman in charge of a measuring station climbs to a rocky mountain bowl in order to read her instruments. Her predecessor entered ice thicknesses into a notebook by hand; she opens her case and finds readings that the sensors have already transmitted of their own accord. He walked on a crust that was hard and faintly bluish underfoot. She works on something spongy that subsides whenever the spikes on her boots bite. Where his notes recorded a clean wall of ice, hers describe a thinned tongue streaked with gravel that crumbles between the fingers. She observes two facing slopes of the same range as well: the shaded one holds, while the one exposed to the full sun surrenders its ice far faster. That difference, she maintains, teaches her more than any overall average.

units: the review deals with a set of photographs given over to drought
the first part shows split soils covered with whitish deposits
the second part shows horizons veiled by the heat
a third part gathers emptied watercourses and abandoned watering gear
the last part shows the people who have stayed on
the reviewer holds this last part to be the finest
the work as a whole keeps clear of lament and of moral lessons
the pictures are ordered so that each one calls for the next
the reviewer reckons the silence of the frames carries more than a speech
text: Seldom has a photographic sequence handled drought with such considerable restraint. The opening series remains low, on the ground itself: clay split into plates, a whitish chalky crust, pale dust lifting at the slightest breath. The second rises away from the soil into the air, where heat veils every distant edge. A third gathers the water that is no longer there, with river beds paved in stones, emptied basins, watering pipes coiled and abandoned where they fell. The final series, and the finest, turns towards the people who have remained behind. Nowhere does the work slip into lamentation or into a lesson on how to live. It offers instead a measured crossing in which one picture calls for the next, and in which the silence inside the frames carries further than any speech could manage.

units: the writer sends word from a measuring post to tell of a repair
he opened the casing at the start of the week
a mineral deposit coated the temperature probe and skewed the readings
he cleaned that probe in an acid bath while watching the time
he then put the instrument back together and checked that the seal held
the curve showed a fixed offset once the thing was running again
so he calibrated the instrument afresh against a reference probe
he cleaned the fouled solar panel and the charging voltage climbed back
the readings have come in without a break ever since
he asks his correspondent to come and see the monitoring board he has set up
text: I said I would write from the measuring post once the sensor was working again, so here it is at last. At the start of the week I opened the casing and found the temperature probe furred over with a chalky deposit that skewed every reading. I soaked it in an acid bath, timing the operation closely, because the stuff attacks metal. Next day I reassembled the instrument and satisfied myself that the seal was holding. Transmission resumed, but the curve sat a fixed step away from where it belonged, so I set it against the reference probe and calibrated it afresh. Then I wiped the dust off the solar panel and the charging voltage climbed straight back. Nothing has dropped out of the record since. Come up to the post whenever you like and I will show you the monitoring board I have set up.

units: a common question concerns the damp that spreads through the walls of older housing
this damp comes from the groundwater rising beneath the footings
rain that falls harder and closer together feeds that rise
concentrated downpours soak packed soils that take in nothing any more
the water then makes for the cellars
a waterproof coating shuts the damp inside the brickwork
brickwork shut in this way crumbles away in patches
the specialists advise drainage laid round the building
they also advise renders that breathe and ground alongside that takes water in
the answer about cost is that acting late comes to more
text: One question comes up at every public meeting: where does the damp spreading through the walls of older housing come from? It comes from the water table pushing up beneath the footings, itself fed by rainfall that now arrives harder and closer together. The next question follows on: what has that to do with the climate? Downpours arrive all at once, the compacted soil absorbs nothing, and the water goes looking for cellars. Then somebody asks whether a waterproof coating will not do the job. It will not: it shuts the damp inside the brickwork, which turns soft and sheds in patches. So what is advised? Drainage laid right round the building, renders that let a wall breathe, ground alongside it that absorbs water. The last question is about cost, and the answer is blunt: leaving it late comes to more.

units: an angler tells an engineer that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season
a brown foam clings to the stones on the bed
the smell grows stronger as the level of the river drops
the engineer explains that a sewage line upstream spills over during storms
the angler objects that the trouble has gone on for too many seasons
the engineer also brings up the run-off from a stock farm on the plateau
the answer takes in a holding basin upstream
it takes in a thick belt of planting along the banks as well
regular checks on what is put into the river are planned
the engineer says the return of the insects will be the sign of improvement
text: On the bank an angler tells the engineer sent to investigate that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season. She asks whether the colour has shifted; he says a brown foam clings to the stones on the bed, and the stench rises whenever the level drops. She explains that a sewage line upstream overflows whenever a storm exceeds what the network can hold. He is unconvinced: the trouble has continued for far too many seasons to hang on storms alone. She grants him that and mentions the stock farm on the plateau, whose run-off drains towards the bed. Then she sets out the answer: a holding basin upstream, a thick belt of planting along both banks, regular checks on whatever is put into the river. Will it run clear again, he asks. The insects will tell him first, she says.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in one valley wood was once burned for every purpose
the air there smelled of smoke and the walls darkened with soot
people took this state of affairs to be ordinary
a dark fuel was later cut out of the rock
the energy yield rose sharply
workshops sprang up and the sky over the working valleys turned hazy
the real turning point lies in the change of scale
a burnt forest can grow back over generations
the carbon drawn from a buried seam cannot be put back there
the older fires used what grew around them whereas the later ones drew on a store
text: Picture a valley where wood went into every fire, from the cooking pot to the forge. Smoke hung in the air, soot darkened the walls, and nobody considered it worth remarking upon. Set that beside what came afterwards, once a dark fuel was being cut out of the rock: the energy yield leapt, workshops multiplied one after another, and the sky above the working valleys turned hazy from dawn until dusk. The turn came with the scale, not with the flame. Burn a forest and it grows back again, given generations enough. Burn a seam that has lain buried and the carbon it releases goes nowhere back. The older fires consumed whatever grew around them; the ones that followed drew upon a store. Watch the flame and the difference hardly shows. Watch what feeds the flame and the difference shows immediately.

units: three workings account for what is happening to the seas
the first working has to do with the heat the water soaks up
warmed water takes more room and lifts the level with no ice melting
the second working is chemical and comes from dissolved carbon dioxide
water turned acid in this way eats at shells and chalky skeletons
the third working has to do with the stirring of the layers of water
the surface layer mixes less with the layers below
this blockage keeps nutrients from the depths away from the plankton
the three workings feed one another
a sea poorer in life holds back less carbon
text: Three workings, taken together, account for what is happening to the seas. The first of them is thermal. Water absorbs an enormous share of what accumulates, and warmed water occupies more room, so the level climbs before a single piece of ice has melted. The second of them is chemical. As more carbon dioxide dissolves, the water turns faintly corrosive, and it eats at the shells and the chalky skeletons that shellfish and corals build for themselves. The third is a matter of stirring, of how the layers mix. A warm skin of surface water mixes far less with the cold beneath, so the nutrients that formerly rose stay down there and leave the drifting plankton hungry. Each works on its own, yet each also feeds the others. A sea impoverished of life holds back less carbon than it formerly did.

units: the woman keeping a mountain refuge had shut her shutters before the sky changed
a warm breath came down off the pass in the middle of the afternoon
a curtain laden with sand then moved up along the path
sand settled even on the tables
the keeper grasped that the wind had carried this dust from dry country far away
rain tinged with ochre fell as night came on
that rain left hardened streaks down the window panes
the snow on the glacier nearby had turned rust-coloured by morning
that snow melted faster than the keeper had ever seen
she wrote the event into her register without foreseeing that it would come again
text: The woman who keeps a mountain refuge had already shut the shutters before the sky gave any sign of turning. By the middle of the afternoon a warm breath came down off the pass, so close that she left the door standing open. Then the slope went dim, a curtain of dust advanced along the path, and grit settled even on the tables inside. The wind, she understood, had carried that dust from arid country far beyond the ridges. Rain came on at nightfall, heavy and stained the colour of ochre, and dried into hardened streaks down the window panes. In the morning the snow on the glacier nearby was no longer white but rust-coloured, and it melted under her eyes faster than she had ever seen snow melt. She wrote the whole episode into her register, with no notion whatever that it would recur.
